King's problems with The Shining range from Jack Torrance (Jack Nicholson) having no arc to the lack of tragedy in the film. Point of order: King has not been entirely down on the film, and in 1980 on The David Letterman Show, began his interview by lauding the movie for having moments that are, "... flawless and beautiful".

King is allowed his opinion, just as anyone is, and you don't have to like The Shining, but King goes a step further. He claims that the three-episode adaptation of The Shining that premiered on ABC in 1997 is the superior version, a claim which is hard to justify if you've seen them both.
Stephen King Prefers The Shining’s TV Remake Because It’s Faithful To His Novel

blocks.c: The Torrance family standing in the snow in The Shining.

blocks.x: One of the main reasons why King prefers the show version of The Shining is better is that the miniseries is more faithful to his novel, and the actor who plays Jack Torrance, Steven Weber, has a better grasp on the character than Nicholson. That's basically the story of Stephen King in the '70s and '80s. He too struggled with substance abuse issues. It's almost an autobiographical story, so any changes to it would probably feel deeply personal and just wrong to King.

I have another theory as to why King didn't like Kubrick's film. King is highly competitive. He's a prolific writer with incredible ambition and energy, and he's a sports lover, with baseball being the center of several of his stories. I would not be surprised if the success of Kubrick's The Shining ticked King off a bit and got his competitive juices going, like a slugger who gets struck out by a Gold Glove pitcher.
Mike Flanagan’s Carrie Is Nothing Like The Book, Yet King Loves It

blocks.c: Summer H. Howell as Carrie White, looking upset

blocks.x: A King adaptation doesn't need to be absolutely faithful for King to like it. Take Mike Flanagan's Carrie. King has come out and called the eight-episode miniseries "brilliant" and "shocking and true" in anticipation of the October 7th premiere date of the show on Prime Video.

Carrie is far from faithful to the source material. The series is a reimagining of the novel, a necessity considering Flanagan needs to fill eight episodes with a story that's one of King's shortest novels. While the storyline may be different, Flanagan has been clear that the themes and ideas remain the same, and it seems that's what counts for King when it comes to The Shining, Carrie, or any other adaptations of his stories.
